newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanian right bids to unseat ex-Communists.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanian right bids to unseat ex-Communists.

text.p: Lithuania's rightist parties, spearheaded by independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis, on Wednesday appealed for popular backing in elections this month in which they hope to unseat the ruling party of ex-communists.
Lithuanians vote in two rounds on October 20 and November 10 in the second general election since the Baltic state of 3.6 million regained its independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.

In 1992, Lithuania set a trend in eastern Europe by returning former Communists to power, dumping Landsbergis' Sajudis, which had led the independence drive, in favour of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) formed from reformist communists.

Landsbergis' Homeland Union, the Christian Democrat Party, with which it wants to form a government, and four other parties signed a declaration in which they appealed for popular support on Wednesday.
In all, 24 parties and 1,351 candidates are running in the election.
"We think that these parties...will be able to form a majority in parliament which will guarantee changes in society," the declaration said.
LDLP leader Algirdas Brazauskas completed the former Communists sweep back into power in February 1993, winning presidential elections against Sajudis-backed candidate Stasys Lozoraitis.

But after fours years in power, the LDLP are fighting popular cynicism about politics in general, a reputation for corruption and croneyism and accusations they reneged on populist promises made when elected.
Landsbergis' Homeland Union is expected to be the largest party in the new parliament but retaking power will not be easy.
Only five or six of the 24 parties contesting the election are expected to get representation in the 141-seat parliament as they have to pass a five percent barrier.
The Homeland Union and the Christian Democrats hoped to form a coalition with the populist Centre Party but it did not sign Wednesday's declaration.

An opinion poll by Baltic Research for newspaper Respublika earlier this month showed support for the Homeland Union at 14.7 percent, the LDLP at 12 percent, the Centre Party at 10.5 percent and the Christian Democrats at 9.3 percent.
But there is still much uncertainty as some 25 percent of those who had decided to vote did not know who they would back.

In the first round, Lithuanians will choose from party lists under a proportional representation system to decide 70 of the parliament seats. In the second round, people vote for individual candidates on a first-past-the-post system to fill the rest of the seats.
Lithuanians are also being asked to vote on three referenda on October 20 including changes to the constitution and compensation for bank deposits.
The LDLP came to power with promises to ease the pain of transformation from Communism but instead followed a path of austerity mapped out by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Its record on the economy has been patchy, having brought down inflation and kept a stable currency but failing to privatise state-owned industries with as much enthusiasm as other reformers in the region.
